**Mindsets Matter: How Beliefs About Facebook Moderate the Association Between Time Spent and Well-Being** (URL: [https://research.facebook.com/publications/mindsets-matter-how-beliefs-about-facebook-moderate-the-association-between-time-spent-and-well-being/](https://research.facebook.com/publications/mindsets-matter-how-beliefs-about-facebook-moderate-the-association-between-time-spent-and-well-being/))   
*(Published April 2022\)*

Summary:  
The paper finds correlation between people’s beliefs about whether social media is good or bad and time spent on social media and well-being. When people perceive Facebook more negatively, the more time they think they spend on the platform, the lower their well-being. When people perceive Facebook more positively, time they think they spend on the platform is not associated with well-being. It also shows that mindsets have a stronger moderating effect when time spent measures are self-reported rather than coming from more objective sources (like server logs), and thus, it is better to log applications or time-use software rather than asking participants for time estimates in future studies. 

* Published work has identified many factors implicated in the connection between social media use and well-being, including (but not limited to) active communication vs. passive use, interactions w/ close friends vs. others, envy, responsiveness to friends’ requests for help, network composition, procrastination, and authenticity  
* People’s beliefs about degree to which social media is good/bad may be driven by endogenous or exogenous sources  
  * Endogenous sources include reflections on one’s prior experiences online, such as being bullied, feeling social comparison, or receiving a kind comment from a friend  
    * In this case, people’s beliefs about social media may be accurate evaluations of its impact based on their own prior use  
  * Exogenous sources include media narratives (e.g., academic and popular press coverage emphasizing that social media is bad for one’s well-being)  
* Time spent on platform, independent of what users are doing on those platforms, is a poor predictor of well-being in and of itself  
  * Additionally, time spent on social media is difficult for people to report accurately and may be biased, in part, by their beliefs about whether their use is good/bad  
* In work that theorizes positive outcomes, the literature focuses on affordances of social media which enable people to find social support among new & existing networks, maintain connections w/ ties that would otherwise have deteriorated over time, and lower the barriers to social connectedness  
  * Information-seeking, uses for entertainment and news, or connecting w/ weak ties (and the informational resources they represent) are also important benefits  
* In work that highlights negative consequences of social media use for various facets of well-being  
  * Consumption as opposed to active connection & communication   
    * E.g., self-esteem issues, one potential pathway presumes that individuals consume content from others that highlights more positive aspects of others’ lives, resulting in negative social comparison  
  * Social media introduces feelings of ostracism or being left out of social activities (FoMO)   
* Important potential moderators:  
  * Active vs. passive use  
    * More active use may be associated with positive outcomes via social connectedness, whereas more passive use may be more associated with well-being (via self-esteem)  
  * Communication partner and effort (e.g., a written comment rather than a single-click Like)   
    * Someone receiving “targeted, composed communication from strong ties” experienced improved well-being  
  * Social comparison orientation (or how people pay attention to the way others behave and their own behavior in kind)  
  * Asking for and providing support   
    * Also known to play a role in social capital benefits people draw from platform use  
* Mindsets are “core assumptions about the nature and operation of things in the world that can help explain differences in people’s thoughts, feelings and behaviors”  
* Prior literature on social media non-use also highlights role of beliefs in whether/how people spend time on social media  
  * E.g., volitionality, disenchantment or disinterest, and resistance are used to characterize different types of social media non-use  
  * Beliefs related to privacy, data misuse, productivity, banality, etc., are identified as motivations and justifications for limiting the use of social media or not using these platforms at all  
* Methods: surveyed Facebook users between June & July, 2019  
  * Combined survey responses w/ server logs of participants’ time spent on Facebook in the four weeks prior to the survey  
  * No identifiable or individual-level data were viewed by researchers  
  * First, research plan was reviewed by five-person panel of experts in the research area, research ethics, law, & policy  
    * Reviewed the proposal for potential benefits, such as improvements for people on Facebook or contributions to general knowledge, as well as participant risks & required regulation adherence (e.g., data privacy, security, or impact to vulnerable populations)  
  * After research was completed, manuscript was reviewed by company prior to publication  
    * No findings were changed in this review  
  * All research questions in the paper were developed by authors prior to the first Facebook review  
* Participants:  
  * N \= 29,284  
  * 50% female, Mean age 34.2  
  * Recruited via invitation to take survey shown at top of their Facebook News Feeds on web and mobile interfaces w/ text: “\<Name\>, we’d like to hear from you. Please tell us about your experience using Facebook.”  
  * Survey response rate: \~2%  
  * Targeted at random samples of people on Facebook in Australia, Brazil, Canada, France, Germany, India, Indonesia, Mexico, Philippines, Spain, Thailand, Turkey, United Kingdom, United States, & Vietnam   
  * On average, participants took \~3 mins to complete survey & were not compensated  
* Survey contained six questions about subjective well-being: one question each in random order on life satisfaction, positive affect, and negative affect followed by one question each on loneliness, social support, and belonging, again in random order  
  * Participants answer two questions eliciting their beliefs about Facebook  
    * “To what extent do you think Facebook is good or bad for society?”  
    * “To what extent do you think Facebook is good or bad for you?”   
  * Responses to both questions were on an 11-point slider w/ labels for:  
    * “Very bad” (0)  
    * “Neutral” (5)  
    * “Very good” (10)  
  * Responses to the two belief questions were highly correlated (r \= 0.69, p \< 0.001) and thus were combined by taking their average  
  * Participants were shown one question from a counter-balanced set of 10 questions about how much time they spent or how many times they checked Facebook  
    * Approximately 3000 participants answered each question  
    * Because the specific self-reported time-spent questions weren’t paper’s main focus, responses were pooled across questions and analyzed in aggregate after converting to standard deviation units, creating comparable “self-reported time-spent” measure for each participant  
* Two sets of linear regressions performed w/ well-being as the outcome: one set using perceived (self-reported) time spent on Facebook, and another using actual time spent on Facebook from the server logs  
  * All regressions controlled for age, gender identity, country, friend count, and account tenure in days  
* Results:  
  ![][image1]  
  * **On average, participants believed that Facebook was moderately good for them personally (*M* \= 6.7 out of 10\) and for society (*M* \= 6.4 out of 10), with a combined belief score of *M* \= 6.6**  
  * **Participants in globally western countries, teens and adults up to age 30, and women generally reported believing that Facebook was worse than people in eastern and global south countries, adults over age 30, and men**  
  * Beliefs about Facebook also varied by friend count, account tenure, & time spent on platform  
    * **People w/ more friends on Facebook, those w/ less tenure on the platform, those who spent more time on the platform according to server logs, and those who perceived spending more time on the platform all reported higher average beliefs about Facebook being good for themselves & society**  
  * **The better people believed Facebook was for them personally, the more likely they were to overestimate how much time they spent on the platform**: not only did they actually spend more time on Facebook than people who believed the platform was bad, they also perceived spending even more time than they actually did  
    * People who believed Facebook was good also reported higher average levels of subjective well-being  
      * Casual direction unknown: it could be that higher well-being causes people to think more positively about Facebook, or the reverse, or that another underlying variable such as having a good day when taking the survey caused people to report higher levels of well-being and more positive beliefs about Facebook  
  * **Participants who perceived spending more time on Facebook (standardized and pooled across all survey questions) reported modestly lower levels of well-being**  
    * **There was a significant interaction between beliefs & perceived time spent**  
    * **When people believed that Facebook was very good for them and for society, time they thought they spent on the platform was not significantly associated w/ their well-being**  
      * **Conversely, when they believed Facebook was bad, the more they thought they used the platform, the lower their well-being**  
  * **Actual time spent had a small negative correlation w/ well-being**  
    * Casual direction is also unknown: it could be that spending more time on Facebook contributes to lower well-being, or it may be that people who have lower levels of well-being try to mitigate this by spending more time on Facebook, e.g., to build connections or entertain themselves  
    * **As before, people's beliefs about whether Facebook is good or bad for themselves or society significantly moderated the association between actual time spent and well-being**  
  * **![][image2]**  
* **When people think that Facebook is good, the time they think they spent on the platform is not associated w/ their subjective well-being**  
  * **Conversely, when they think that Facebook is bad and use it more, they report lower well-being**  
    * **This moderation effect of beliefs is stronger when the time spent data is self-reported than when it comes from server logs**  
* Different use patterns, cultural norms around technology use, privacy perceptions, differences in online experiences and the emphasis of social media’s impact in local media may play a contributing role in demographic differences in beliefs about Facebook  
* **Beliefs about whether Facebook was good or bad had a 3.4x stronger association with well-being than self-reported time spent on Facebook did**  
* Experimental limitations: (there are more but here are a few of the major ones)   
  * “Demand effects,” or potential error introduced by changes in participant behavior because of cues or expectations about appropriate or expected behavior   
  * Mismatch between people’s self-reports of their social media use and objective indicators is well-documented \-\> study suggests that beliefs about a social media platform may exacerbate this self-report error, because people who thought that Facebook was better were more likely to overestimate their Facebook use  
  * Study is correlational, not causational\!
